nodes.title: Amazon VPC: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A VPC is a logically isolated network inside an AWS region. You define the IP range, create subnets in multiple AZs, route tables decide where packets go, and security groups + NACLs filter what's allowed. Most networking exam Qs are VPC-shaped.

flashcards.front: Public vs private subnet — what makes the difference?
flashcards.back: Routing. A 'public' subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway (0.0.0.0/0 → IGW). A 'private' subnet doesn't — its instances can reach the internet only via a NAT Gateway (outbound) or VPC endpoint (to specific AWS services). The subnet's CIDR doesn't determine its category — the route table does.

flashcards.front: Security group vs network ACL — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Security group: stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), applied per ENI / instance, default deny, allow rules only. NACL: stateless (must allow return traffic explicitly), applied per subnet, supports allow and deny rules, evaluated in numbered order. SGs handle 95% of cases; NACLs add a deny-list at the subnet edge.

flashcards.front: What's a NAT Gateway for?
flashcards.back: Lets instances in a private subnet initiate outbound internet traffic (package updates, API calls to public endpoints) while remaining unreachable from the internet. The NAT replaces the source IP with its own elastic IP. One per AZ for HA — they're zonal, not regional.

flashcards.front: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway — when to scale up?
flashcards.back: Peering connects two VPCs (mesh: N VPCs need N×(N-1)/2 peerings). It's free per-GB but doesn't transit. Transit Gateway is a hub: many VPCs and on-prem VPNs all connect to it, full transitive routing. Use peering up to ~5 VPCs; switch to TGW when the mesh becomes painful.

questions.q: An application team exposes a Kubernetes service via an internal NLB in VPC-A. Consumers in VPC-B (different AWS account, same Region) must access this service privately without VPC peering or Transit Gateway attachments. Which solution is appropriate?
choices: Attach both VPCs to a Transit Gateway and use TGW route tables to permit only the consumer subnets to reach the producer service
Create a VPC peering connection between VPC-A and VPC-B and add the reciprocal routes on both sides' route tables
Share a Route 53 private hosted zone across the two accounts so VPC-B can resolve and then connect to the NLB DNS name
Create a VPC Endpoint Service (PrivateLink) on the producer NLB in VPC-A and create an Interface Endpoint in VPC-B
questions.explanation: AWS PrivateLink (Endpoint Service backed by an NLB on the producer side, Interface Endpoint on the consumer side) is purpose-built for cross-account service exposure without VPC-level connectivity, avoiding CIDR-overlap concerns and exposing only the specific service. Peering and TGW give whole-network connectivity (more than required) and are explicitly excluded. A shared Route 53 private hosted zone only resolves names — it provides no underlying private network path.

questions.q: A company wants to use Interface VPC Endpoints (PrivateLink) to access Amazon S3 from within a VPC without going through the public internet. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) for S3 are available only in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and are not offered in any of the standard commercial Regions
S3 access from a private subnet always requires a NAT Gateway for the data path, regardless of whether a VPC endpoint exists
S3 Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) are supported and allow private access from on-premises and peered VPCs, complementing free Gateway Endpoints
Gateway Endpoints are the only supported way to reach S3 privately from a VPC, and Interface Endpoints for S3 do not exist
questions.explanation: AWS provides both S3 Gateway Endpoints (free, route-table based, reachable only from within the VPC) and S3 Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink, hourly + data-processing charge, reachable from on-premises via DX/VPN and from peered VPCs). The two coexist and many architectures use both. Interface endpoints for S3 are generally available, not GovCloud-only. A NAT Gateway is required only when you don't have any endpoint and want to reach S3 over the internet path.

questions.q: A company wants to enforce that all VPC endpoints created in member accounts must use an endpoint policy restricting access to specific S3 buckets. Which AWS service can enforce this at scale across accounts?
choices: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) distributing shared endpoint-policy templates to every one of the member accounts in the organization
AWS Shield Advanced protection policies applied at the VPC endpoint level within each member account
AWS Organizations SCPs (to deny non-compliant endpoint creation) combined with AWS Config rules (to detect drift) and remediation
AWS Firewall Manager endpoint policies pushed organization-wide to every member account automatically
questions.explanation: Organization-wide endpoint-policy enforcement is achieved by combining SCPs (deny the creation of endpoints without the required policy condition), AWS Config rules (continuously detect non-compliant endpoints), and automated remediation via SSM/Lambda. Firewall Manager covers SG, WAF, Network Firewall, and DNS Firewall policies — not generic endpoint policies. RAM shares resources; it does not enforce policy compliance. Shield Advanced is DDoS-only.

questions.q: A company has a private ALB in a VPC and wants to expose it to customers over PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints). What must the company configure?
choices: Use Amazon API Gateway private endpoints to expose the ALB to the consumer VPCs
Create a Network Load Balancer with ALB-type targets pointing at the ALB, then create a VPC Endpoint Service on the NLB
Configure PrivateLink directly at the ALB listener level without any intermediate NLB
Create a VPC Endpoint Service directly from the ALB itself and share it with each of the consumer accounts that needs to reach the service
questions.explanation: VPC Endpoint Services on the PrivateLink provider side must be backed by NLB or GWLB. Since 2021, NLB supports ALB-type targets, so the producer creates an NLB that targets the ALB and then creates the VPC Endpoint Service on that NLB. Consumers create Interface Endpoints to reach it. ALB cannot back an Endpoint Service directly, and the listener has no PrivateLink toggle. API Gateway is for API publishing, not generic L7 service exposure.

questions.q: A company has an EC2 instance in a private subnet without internet access. It must reach an Amazon Kinesis stream privately. What is the simplest solution?
choices: Create an Interface VPC Endpoint (PrivateLink) for Kinesis in the same VPC so the instance reaches Kinesis privately
Deploy a NAT Gateway in a public subnet and route the private subnet's traffic out through it
Use VPC peering to another VPC that already hosts a Kinesis Interface Endpoint and route through it
Attach an Internet Gateway and assign a public IP so the instance reaches Kinesis over the internet
questions.explanation: Kinesis supports PrivateLink Interface Endpoints, which create ENIs in the VPC that resolve to private IPs — the EC2 instance reaches Kinesis without any internet path. A NAT Gateway works but adds cost and routes traffic over the public internet, contradicting the 'private' requirement. Peering for the sole purpose of accessing Kinesis is unneeded complexity. IGW + public IP defeats the private-subnet design entirely.

questions.q: A company has an S3 bucket with Block Public Access enabled and wants to allow only one specific VPC to access it, while explicitly denying requests from any other VPC or the internet. Which policy configuration enforces this?
choices: Enable S3 object-level ACLs and set every object's ACL to private so that only the single approved VPC is able to read the bucket contents
Use a VPC Endpoint Policy that allows access to every S3 bucket from the endpoint's own VPC
Use network ACLs to restrict the S3-bound traffic at the subnet level to the one approved VPC
Use a bucket policy with an aws:SourceVpce (or aws:SourceVpc) condition that allows the specific endpoint/VPC and denies everything else
questions.explanation: S3 bucket policies support the aws:SourceVpce and aws:SourceVpc condition keys to restrict access to a specific VPC endpoint or VPC. Combining an Allow for the specific VPCe with an explicit Deny for any other source enforces the requirement at the bucket level. ACLs are coarse and overlapping with Block Public Access settings. Endpoint policies control what the endpoint allows out — they don't constrain what reaches the bucket from other paths. NACLs operate on IP traffic at subnet boundaries and cannot identify S3 callers semantically.

questions.q: A company has a VPC endpoint (Interface) for an AWS service and wants to restrict which IAM principals can use it. Which mechanism enforces this at the endpoint level?
choices: AWS Organizations SCPs scoped specifically to the individual VPC endpoint's resource ID
An AWS RAM resource share whose permission list explicitly enumerates the IAM principals that are allowed to use the interface endpoint
A VPC Endpoint Policy — a resource-based policy attached to the endpoint that restricts the principals and actions through it
Security group rules on the endpoint that match traffic against the caller's IAM principal ARN
questions.explanation: VPC Endpoint Policies are resource-based policies attached directly to the endpoint and are the right tool to restrict which IAM principals can perform which actions via the endpoint. Security groups operate on network attributes (IPs/ports), not IAM principals. SCPs are organization-level guardrails on identities, not endpoint configuration. RAM is for resource sharing across accounts, not access control on an endpoint.

nodes.title: Amazon CloudFront: Key Ideas
nodes.content: CloudFront is AWS's CDN — caches your origin's content at 400+ edge locations worldwide so users get low-latency hits. The exam tests origins, cache behaviors, TTLs, invalidation, signed URLs, and the difference between viewer and origin requests.

flashcards.front: What can CloudFront use as an origin?
flashcards.back: S3 bucket (typical for static sites), an ALB / API Gateway / Lambda function URL, an EC2 instance with a public IP, or any HTTP origin including on-prem servers. One distribution can have multiple origins with cache behaviors routing by path (e.g., `/api/*` → ALB, `/*` → S3).

flashcards.front: Cache key — what determines whether two requests hit the same cache entry?
flashcards.back: The cache key is composed from the URL path plus any policy-specified headers, cookies, and query strings. By default it's just path. To vary by `Accept-Language` for example, add it to the cache policy. Beware: too many cache-key dimensions explodes cache size and lowers hit rate.

flashcards.front: How do you invalidate cached content?
flashcards.back: Two options. (1) Cache invalidation API: pay per path invalidated — fine for emergencies, expensive at scale ('/*' is one path, but full bypass for ~15 min). (2) Versioned URLs: rename `style.css` to `style-v3.css` on every deploy — costs nothing, immediate, doesn't disturb the existing cache. Always prefer versioned URLs.

flashcards.front: What's a signed URL / signed cookie for?
flashcards.back: Time-limited access to private content. Signed URL: hand out a unique URL with a signature parameter that grants access until a specific timestamp. Signed cookie: same idea but the credential is in a cookie covering multiple URLs (good for streaming where the player issues many requests). Use IAM-based access (OAC) when content is non-public AND served only via CloudFront.

questions.q: A media streaming company uses CloudFront with an S3 origin serving premium content. Requirements: (1) block direct access to the S3 bucket so that content is only accessible via CloudFront, (2) support signed URLs with short-lived tokens, (3) block countries under trade restrictions. Which combination implements all requirements?
choices: Validate access tokens with Lambda@Edge, control object access using S3 pre-signed URLs, and block restricted countries with AWS Shield Advanced geo policies
Restrict the S3 bucket policy to the CloudFront service principal, add a WAF geo-match rule for restricted countries, and meet the token requirement with CloudFront signed cookies
Configure Origin Access Control (OAC) on the S3 origin, use CloudFront signed URLs for short-lived tokens, and apply CloudFront geo restriction to block restricted countries
Use a legacy CloudFront OAI, enable S3 Block Public Access on the bucket, and apply CloudFront field-level encryption to protect the premium content
questions.explanation: Origin Access Control (OAC) is the modern replacement for OAI; it supports SigV4 and SSE-KMS and is the AWS-recommended way to lock S3 access to CloudFront. CloudFront signed URLs are the canonical short-lived token mechanism. CloudFront geo restriction (or a WAF geo-match rule) handles country blocking. Signed cookies satisfy session-style auth but the requirement specifies signed URLs. Shield Advanced is DDoS protection — not geo-blocking. OAI + field-level encryption misses the URL-token requirement entirely.

questions.q: A company has an ALB behind CloudFront and needs to ensure CloudFront viewers cannot bypass CloudFront and hit the ALB directly. Which method provides this enforcement with the least maintenance overhead?
choices: Place the ALB in a private subnet with neither a NAT Gateway nor an internet gateway route, assuming that only CloudFront can then reach it
Configure CloudFront to add a custom HTTP header with a secret value and add a WAF rule on the ALB that allows only requests carrying that header
Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer in front of the ALB to transparently inspect and drop any non-CloudFront source traffic
Run a scheduled Lambda that keeps the ALB security group updated with the CloudFront edge IPs parsed from ip-ranges.json
questions.explanation: The maintenance-light, AWS-recommended patterns are (a) the AWS Managed Prefix List for CloudFront origin-facing IPs in the ALB SG, or (b) CloudFront injecting a custom secret header and a WAF rule on the ALB validating it. The custom-header + WAF approach is robust and has no Lambda or IP-list to maintain. Maintaining IPs via Lambda is brittle and outdated. GWLB is not the right tool. A private ALB with no NAT isn't reachable from CloudFront either, so it would block legitimate traffic too.

questions.q: A company uses CloudFront in front of multiple origins and wants to selectively modify viewer request headers (to add a geolocation header) before they reach the origin. Requirements: extremely low-latency, simple logic, no package dependencies. Which feature fits best?
choices: Lambda@Edge origin-request triggers running Node.js code at the regional edge caches
CloudFront Functions running at every edge location for sub-millisecond header manipulation
CloudFront Origin Shield with transformation rules applied at the shield cache layer
AWS WAF custom response headers configured directly on the web ACL
questions.explanation: CloudFront Functions execute at every edge location (600+) with sub-millisecond startup and are designed for lightweight header manipulation, URL rewrites, and simple auth checks — at a fraction of Lambda@Edge cost. Lambda@Edge supports richer logic and Node.js packages but runs only at regional edge caches with higher cold-start and cost. Origin Shield is an extra cache layer, not a transformation engine. WAF custom response headers are for WAF actions, not generic request rewrites.

questions.q: A company has a CloudFront distribution serving content from multiple origins globally. They notice that requests during traffic spikes sometimes bypass the regional cache and hit the origin directly, increasing origin load. Which feature reduces origin load during spikes?
choices: Enable Lambda@Edge on viewer-response events to coalesce the duplicate cache misses
Use CloudFront Functions to rewrite responses so that cache keys collapse during the spikes
Enable CloudFront Origin Shield in a Region close to the origin to consolidate edge cache misses
Increase the TTLs on the distribution's cache behaviors to absorb the spike traffic
questions.explanation: CloudFront Origin Shield is an additional centralized cache layer that consolidates requests from all edge locations into a single shielded cache near the origin — dramatically reducing origin load during cache-miss spikes and improving cache hit ratios. Higher TTLs help but aren't always acceptable for dynamic content. CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge transform requests/responses; they don't consolidate cache misses.

questions.q: A company uses AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to issue public TLS certificates for ALBs and CloudFront. They want to automatically rotate certificates without manual intervention. Which statement is accurate?
choices: ACM Private CA certificates auto-renew automatically, but public ACM certificates can never be auto-renewed by the service under any circumstances
Public ACM certificates must be manually rotated by the customer roughly every 13 months before expiry
DNS-validated public ACM certificates used by integrated services auto-renew before expiry while the validation CNAMEs remain in DNS
Auto-renewal of public ACM certificates is only available when AWS Shield Advanced is enabled on the account
questions.explanation: ACM automatically renews public certificates used by integrated AWS services as long as DNS validation CNAME records remain in DNS — no manual action needed. Email-validated certs are harder to auto-renew because they require human confirmation. Shield Advanced is unrelated. ACM Private CA certificates also benefit from auto-renewal when used via integrated services. The 'never auto-renew' claim for public certificates is simply false.

questions.q: A company wants to monitor ISP-level performance issues affecting their internet-facing applications worldwide and automatically correlate them with their AWS resources. Which AWS service provides this capability?
choices: Amazon CloudWatch Internet Monitor, which uses AWS global observability to detect ISP-level disruptions and tie them to the workloads
AWS Global Accelerator endpoint health checks that run continuously against each of the application's regional endpoint groups worldwide
Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries probing the application from a set of selected Regions
AWS Config managed rules evaluating the configuration of the internet-facing resources
questions.explanation: Amazon CloudWatch Internet Monitor uses AWS's global observability data to detect ISP-level and internet-wide performance disruptions, and correlates them automatically with the customer's workloads (CloudFront, ALB, NLB, EC2, WorkSpaces, VPCs). Synthetics canaries probe specific endpoints but don't aggregate ISP-level signals. Global Accelerator health checks monitor endpoint availability, not ISP health. AWS Config evaluates configuration compliance — not internet path performance.

nodes.title: Route53: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Route53. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A financial services company needs a hybrid DNS architecture where on-premises DNS servers can resolve records in AWS Route 53 private hosted zones, and AWS resources can resolve internal company domains hosted on-premises. What is the correct configuration?
flashcards.back: Route 53 Resolver endpoints solve hybrid DNS. Inbound endpoints terminate DNS queries from on-premises (for AWS private zones), and outbound endpoints forward queries from AWS to on-prem resolvers using domain-scoped forwarding rules. Public hosted zones are not appropriate for internal names (and would expose them). Custom BIND on EC2 works but is unmanaged and not the AWS-recommended pattern. The Amazon-provided resolver at VPC+2 alone cannot forward to on-premises without an outbound endpoint.

flashcards.front: A company uses Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall to block requests to known malicious domains. They want high-confidence AWS-managed blocklists that are continuously updated. Which configuration should be used?
flashcards.back: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall integrates AWS Managed Domain Lists (malware, botnet C&C) that are continuously curated by AWS. You associate them into a rule group with action BLOCK and attach the rule group to the VPC. GuardDuty detects malicious DNS activity but does not natively block at the resolver layer. Manual custom lists work but require ongoing maintenance. Network Firewall can inspect DNS payloads but is not the AWS-managed-blocklist mechanism the question asks about.

flashcards.front: A regulated customer requires all DNS traffic within their VPCs to go through their on-premises DNS servers for compliance logging. Which Route 53 Resolver configuration delivers this?
flashcards.back: An outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for the root '.' domain forwards every query to the configured on-premises targets, associated to the relevant VPCs. Inbound endpoints handle the opposite direction (on-prem → AWS). Disabling VPC DNS entirely would break internal AWS resolution (e.g., VPC interface endpoints). A private hosted zone is a zone, not a forwarder.

flashcards.front: A global company uses Route 53 with latency-based routing and health checks for an application deployed in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1. Users in Singapore report being routed to eu-west-1 even though ap-southeast-1 is healthy. What is the most likely cause?
flashcards.back: Latency-based routing returns the record with the lowest latency among healthy records. If Singapore users end up at eu-west-1, the ap-southeast-1 record is most likely either failing its associated health check or has the wrong Region tag, so it is excluded from selection. There is no per-Region toggle for latency routing, and it is not us-east-1-only. There is no 'latency base' alias configuration.

questions.q: A financial services company needs a hybrid DNS architecture where on-premises DNS servers can resolve records in AWS Route 53 private hosted zones, and AWS resources can resolve internal company domains hosted on-premises. What is the correct configuration?
choices: Host both the AWS private zones and the internal company zones in Route 53 public hosted zones and configure NS delegations between them for cross-resolution
Create Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints for on-premises queries into AWS plus outbound endpoints with forwarding rules for the on-premises domains
Run BIND name servers on EC2 instances in each AZ and point the VPC DHCP option set at them so they recursively resolve both directions
Enable DNS hostnames and DNS resolution on the VPC and rely on the Amazon-provided resolver at VPC+2 to forward queries to the on-premises servers
questions.explanation: Route 53 Resolver endpoints solve hybrid DNS. Inbound endpoints terminate DNS queries from on-premises (for AWS private zones), and outbound endpoints forward queries from AWS to on-prem resolvers using domain-scoped forwarding rules. Public hosted zones are not appropriate for internal names (and would expose them). Custom BIND on EC2 works but is unmanaged and not the AWS-recommended pattern. The Amazon-provided resolver at VPC+2 alone cannot forward to on-premises without an outbound endpoint.

questions.q: A company uses Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall to block requests to known malicious domains. They want high-confidence AWS-managed blocklists that are continuously updated. Which configuration should be used?
choices: Create a custom Route 53 DNS Firewall domain list and manually keep it updated from publicly available commercial threat feeds
Feed Amazon GuardDuty DNS findings into the resolver layer so that malicious queries are blocked automatically
Associate the AWS Managed Domain Lists (malware, botnet C&C) into a DNS Firewall rule group with a BLOCK action, attached to the VPC
Use AWS Network Firewall with stateful Suricata rules that match the malicious domains inside the DNS query payload
questions.explanation: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall integrates AWS Managed Domain Lists (malware, botnet C&C) that are continuously curated by AWS. You associate them into a rule group with action BLOCK and attach the rule group to the VPC. GuardDuty detects malicious DNS activity but does not natively block at the resolver layer. Manual custom lists work but require ongoing maintenance. Network Firewall can inspect DNS payloads but is not the AWS-managed-blocklist mechanism the question asks about.

questions.q: A regulated customer requires all DNS traffic within their VPCs to go through their on-premises DNS servers for compliance logging. Which Route 53 Resolver configuration delivers this?
choices: Use a Route 53 private hosted zone with conditional forwarding rules configured through a VPC association to the on-premises resolvers
Disable the VPC's DNS resolution and point the DHCP option set at the on-premises DNS servers for every lookup
Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for the root '.' domain that targets the on-premises resolvers
Create a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC that simply points at the on-premises DNS servers
questions.explanation: An outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for the root '.' domain forwards every query to the configured on-premises targets, associated to the relevant VPCs. Inbound endpoints handle the opposite direction (on-prem → AWS). Disabling VPC DNS entirely would break internal AWS resolution (e.g., VPC interface endpoints). A private hosted zone is a zone, not a forwarder.

questions.q: A global company uses Route 53 with latency-based routing and health checks for an application deployed in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1. Users in Singapore report being routed to eu-west-1 even though ap-southeast-1 is healthy. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The ap-southeast-1 record is failing its health check or has the wrong Region tag, so Route 53 excludes it from selection
Route 53 latency-based routing is supported only for resource records that are physically hosted in the us-east-1 Region
Latency-based routing was switched off for ap-southeast-1 by an account-level configuration setting
The ap-southeast-1 record is missing the required Asia-Pacific 'latency base' value in its alias target
questions.explanation: Latency-based routing returns the record with the lowest latency among healthy records. If Singapore users end up at eu-west-1, the ap-southeast-1 record is most likely either failing its associated health check or has the wrong Region tag, so it is excluded from selection. There is no per-Region toggle for latency routing, and it is not us-east-1-only. There is no 'latency base' alias configuration.

questions.q: A company's internal Route 53 private hosted zone contains records for 'corp.internal'. A new VPC in a different account needs to resolve these records. Which mechanism allows this?
choices: Create a public hosted zone delegation for corp.internal shared between the two accounts
Associate the existing private hosted zone with the new VPC using cross-account VPC association authorization
Deploy a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the owner account and point the new VPC at it
Configure VPC peering only, since peering shares the private DNS namespace automatically
questions.explanation: Private hosted zones can be associated with VPCs in different accounts using cross-account authorization: the zone owner runs create-vpc-association-authorization and the VPC owner runs associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone. Public delegation is for public zones, not internal names. Peering provides network connectivity but does not share private DNS. Inbound endpoints terminate on-prem queries into AWS, which is not what's needed here.

nodes.title: BGP: Key Ideas
nodes.content: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol of the internet. It runs between autonomous systems (ASes) and is a path-vector protocol — instead of a metric, each route carries the full list of ASes it has traversed.

flashcards.front: eBGP vs iBGP — what's different?
flashcards.back: eBGP runs between routers in different ASes; it's how the internet is glued together. iBGP runs between routers inside the same AS — it carries external routes to internal routers. iBGP requires a full mesh (or route reflectors) because routes learned via iBGP are NOT re-advertised to other iBGP peers.

flashcards.front: What is AS_PATH and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: AS_PATH is the list of autonomous systems a route has traversed, prepended at each AS boundary. It's the primary loop-prevention mechanism (a router rejects a route already containing its own AS) and the second tie-breaker in BGP best-path selection — shorter path wins.

flashcards.front: BGP best-path attributes — name the top three.
flashcards.back: (1) Highest LOCAL_PREF wins (locally configured 'prefer this exit'). (2) Shortest AS_PATH. (3) Lowest ORIGIN code (IGP < EGP < incomplete). Then MED, then eBGP > iBGP, then lowest IGP cost, then router-ID tie-breaker. LOCAL_PREF is how you steer outbound; AS_PATH prepending is how you influence inbound.

flashcards.front: Why does BGP need a route reflector?
flashcards.back: iBGP requires a full mesh (every router peers with every other) — O(n²) sessions, doesn't scale. A route reflector breaks the rule: it re-advertises iBGP routes to its clients. Clients only peer with the RR. One RR + 100 clients = 100 sessions vs. 5,000 for a full mesh.

questions.q: A company has deployed Transit Gateway with 50 VPC attachments. They observe that some VPC-to-VPC traffic fails while other flows succeed. On investigation, the destination VPC's TGW attachment is visible in the TGW but its CIDR is not in the source TGW route table. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The source VPC security groups are dropping the ephemeral return traffic, so the connection only appears to fail intermittently
The TGW attachment has appliance mode enabled, which is suppressing dynamic route propagation for that particular VPC
The destination VPC attachment is not propagated to the source TGW route table and no static route has been added
The destination VPC has DNS resolution disabled at the VPC level, so name resolution fails even though routing is correct
questions.explanation: Transit Gateway route tables are populated either by propagation (dynamic, pulling CIDRs from attached VPCs) or by static routes. If a VPC attachment is associated with a route table but its CIDR is neither propagated nor statically added, the destination simply isn't reachable from that table. Security groups affect packet filtering, not the TGW route table. Appliance mode preserves flow symmetry; it doesn't remove propagated routes. VPC DNS settings don't affect TGW routing at all.

questions.q: A company requires that traffic between two ENIs in the same VPC must pass through a firewall appliance in a shared services VPC. The firewalls require symmetric flow processing (the same appliance must see both directions of a flow). When using Transit Gateway, which feature ensures symmetric routing?
choices: Enable TGW appliance mode on the attachment that hosts the firewall appliances
Disable route propagation on the inspection route table and rely only on static routes
Configure ECMP on the TGW route table with deterministic per-AZ hashing of flows
Enable BGP multipath on the TGW VPN attachments to pin the forwarding path
questions.explanation: Transit Gateway appliance mode is enabled on the attachment of the inspection VPC; once on, TGW keeps both directions of a flow on the same Availability Zone, so the same stateful appliance instance sees the full bidirectional flow. ECMP by default would hash directions independently and break stateful inspection. BGP multipath applies to VPN attachments and doesn't solve the AZ-affinity problem. Disabling propagation has no bearing on symmetric AZ pinning.

questions.q: A company needs to share a Transit Gateway across 25 AWS accounts in an AWS Organization to attach VPCs from each account. Which service enables this sharing model?
choices: Cross-account IAM roles in the TGW owner account granting ec2:AttachTransitGateway permissions to each member
AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) sharing the Transit Gateway with the Organization or specific OUs
AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) configured to allow cross-account TGW attachment
AWS PrivateLink, by exposing the Transit Gateway as a VPC endpoint service to the consumer accounts
questions.explanation: AWS RAM is the standard mechanism for sharing resources — Transit Gateways, subnets, License Manager configurations, Resolver rules, and more — across accounts or entire organizations/OUs. Cross-account IAM roles are about API-call delegation, not resource sharing for attachment. SCPs are organization-level guardrails and don't share resources. PrivateLink is for exposing services backed by NLB/GWLB; you can't expose a TGW as an endpoint service.

questions.q: A company is configuring a Transit Gateway Connect attachment to integrate SD-WAN appliances with AWS. Which protocol is used between the TGW Connect attachment and the SD-WAN virtual appliances?
choices: GENEVE encapsulation with dynamic route insertion via the TGW control plane
VXLAN with an EVPN control plane providing multi-tenant isolation
IPsec using ESP encapsulation in tunnel mode for each appliance
GRE tunnels combined with BGP over the GRE for dynamic route exchange
questions.explanation: Transit Gateway Connect uses GRE tunnels for transport and BGP (running over the GRE tunnels) for dynamic route exchange with SD-WAN appliances — providing higher performance and simpler operation than IPsec Site-to-Site VPN, which has to terminate IPsec per tunnel. GENEVE is GWLB's protocol. VXLAN/EVPN is a data-center fabric construct, not used here.

questions.q: A company uses Transit Gateway inter-Region peering between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 to connect VPCs. What is true about TGW inter-Region peering?
choices: TGW peering is supported strictly within a single Region and cannot connect Transit Gateways that are located in different Regions at all
TGW inter-Region peering rides the encrypted AWS backbone, but routing is static — you add explicit static routes on both route tables
TGW inter-Region peering requires a Direct Connect Gateway to serve as the transit between the Regions
TGW peering exchanges routes dynamically using BGP between the two peered Transit Gateways
questions.explanation: Inter-Region TGW peering traffic rides the AWS global backbone and is encrypted. Crucially, there is no BGP between peered TGWs: you must add static routes pointing at the peering attachment on both sides — a frequent exam trap. It works across Regions (that's the whole point), does not need a Direct Connect Gateway, and does not use dynamic routing between TGWs.

nodes.title: Amazon VPC: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A VPC is a logically isolated network inside an AWS region. You define the IP range, create subnets in multiple AZs, route tables decide where packets go, and security groups + NACLs filter what's allowed. Most networking exam Qs are VPC-shaped.

flashcards.front: Public vs private subnet — what makes the difference?
flashcards.back: Routing. A 'public' subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway (0.0.0.0/0 → IGW). A 'private' subnet doesn't — its instances can reach the internet only via a NAT Gateway (outbound) or VPC endpoint (to specific AWS services). The subnet's CIDR doesn't determine its category — the route table does.

flashcards.front: Security group vs network ACL — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Security group: stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), applied per ENI / instance, default deny, allow rules only. NACL: stateless (must allow return traffic explicitly), applied per subnet, supports allow and deny rules, evaluated in numbered order. SGs handle 95% of cases; NACLs add a deny-list at the subnet edge.

flashcards.front: What's a NAT Gateway for?
flashcards.back: Lets instances in a private subnet initiate outbound internet traffic (package updates, API calls to public endpoints) while remaining unreachable from the internet. The NAT replaces the source IP with its own elastic IP. One per AZ for HA — they're zonal, not regional.

flashcards.front: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway — when to scale up?
flashcards.back: Peering connects two VPCs (mesh: N VPCs need N×(N-1)/2 peerings). It's free per-GB but doesn't transit. Transit Gateway is a hub: many VPCs and on-prem VPNs all connect to it, full transitive routing. Use peering up to ~5 VPCs; switch to TGW when the mesh becomes painful.

questions.q: A customer has a VPC with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 and needs to add more IP space without changing existing subnets. They also want to use the new space for EKS pods. Which approach is correct?
choices: Add a secondary CIDR block (for example 100.64.0.0/16 from RFC 6598 shared-address space) to the VPC and create new subnets for EKS pod IPs
Add a /22 block from the 172.16.0.0/12 range, which is described as the only range EKS will accept for additional pod IP addresses
Resize the primary CIDR in place from 10.0.0.0/16 to 10.0.0.0/15 so that all of the existing subnets immediately gain more usable addresses
Create a second VPC dedicated to the EKS pods and connect it to the original VPC using VPC peering
questions.explanation: VPCs support secondary CIDR blocks (5 by default, raisable to 50). Using 100.64.0.0/10 (RFC 6598) is a well-known pattern for EKS pod IPs because it preserves scarce RFC1918 space while still being private. You cannot shrink/grow the primary CIDR mask in place. EKS works with any valid RFC1918 or RFC 6598 range — it's not restricted to 172.16.0.0/12. Peering a new VPC adds connectivity overhead when a secondary CIDR solves it directly.

questions.q: A company operates 3 VPCs (A, B, C) with CIDRs 10.1.0.0/16, 10.2.0.0/16, and 10.1.0.0/16 respectively. They want to connect all three. Which limitation applies?
choices: VPC peering does support overlapping CIDRs between VPC A and VPC C as long as the route tables declare which side wins per prefix
AWS Cloud WAN automatically resolves overlapping CIDRs by applying built-in NAT inside the core network
Native peering, TGW, and Cloud WAN require non-overlapping CIDRs, so VPC A and C cannot both connect without re-CIDR or PrivateLink
Transit Gateway automatically resolves overlapping CIDRs by applying implicit NAT on the VPC attachment
questions.explanation: All native AWS L3 VPC connectivity options — peering, Transit Gateway, Cloud WAN, Direct Connect, VPN — require non-overlapping CIDRs because routing is destination-IP based. The only way to bridge overlapping CIDRs without re-IP is service-level abstraction such as PrivateLink (consumer accesses the producer via an ENI in the consumer's CIDR) or self-managed NAT appliances. None of peering/TGW/Cloud WAN performs implicit NAT.

questions.q: An organization requires that all outbound internet traffic from EKS pods in a VPC originate from specific static IPs so that SaaS vendors can allowlist them. Which architecture accomplishes this?
choices: Assign an Elastic IP directly to each EKS worker node and have the SaaS vendors allowlist every node IP
Place a Network Load Balancer in front of all outbound pod traffic and present its associated IP addresses to the SaaS vendors for allowlisting
Route all pod egress through CloudFront and give the SaaS vendors the published CloudFront IP ranges
Use a NAT Gateway in each public subnet (each with an Elastic IP) and route pod egress through it; the NAT EIPs are the static outbound IPs
questions.explanation: NAT Gateways present their associated Elastic IPs as the outbound source IP. Routing private-subnet pod traffic through NAT Gateways gives SaaS vendors a small, stable list of EIPs to allowlist. Assigning EIPs to worker nodes makes the IP list grow with autoscaling. NLB is for inbound traffic, not source-NAT for outbound. CloudFront is a content-delivery network, not an egress proxy for arbitrary traffic.

questions.q: A company needs high availability for outbound traffic from a VPC with two private subnets across two AZs. Which NAT Gateway design ensures AZ-level fault isolation?
choices: Deploy a single NAT Gateway in AZ-A and route both of the private subnets to it to save on cost
Deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ in a public subnet of that AZ, and route each private subnet to the NAT Gateway in its own AZ via 0.0.0.0/0
Run NAT instances in an Auto Scaling group that spans both Availability Zones with automatic health-based failover configured between them
Route the private subnets straight to an Internet Gateway without using any NAT at all
questions.explanation: NAT Gateways are AZ-scoped. For AZ fault isolation, deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ in that AZ's public subnet and route each private subnet to the NAT Gateway in the same AZ — losing one AZ doesn't affect the other. A single NAT Gateway creates a cross-AZ SPOF and incurs cross-AZ data-transfer charges. NAT instances are legacy. IGW directly from private subnets does not provide outbound source NAT (and private subnets by definition aren't routed to an IGW).

questions.q: A company operates a VPC with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 and needs to launch a new service that requires more than 65,000 IPs. Rather than re-architect, they want to add more address space. Which approach is correct?
choices: You cannot extend a VPC's address space at all; you must build an entirely new VPC and migrate every existing workload over to it instead
You must convert the VPC into a RAM-shared VPC to unlock the additional IP address capacity
VPCs support secondary CIDR blocks (up to 5 by default, raisable to 50), so add a secondary CIDR and create new subnets there
Cloud WAN automatically expands the CIDR ranges of attached VPCs on demand as they fill up
questions.explanation: A VPC supports secondary CIDR blocks (5 by default, raisable to 50), which is exactly the mechanism for extending IP space without creating a new VPC. Shared VPC (RAM-shared subnets) is about cross-account subnet sharing, not capacity expansion. Cloud WAN orchestrates connectivity; it doesn't grow CIDRs. The 'must create a new VPC' claim is false — secondary CIDRs make that unnecessary.

nodes.title: VPN and secure connectivity: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A VPN tunnels private traffic over the public internet, encrypting it end-to-end. Site-to-site VPNs connect networks (e.g., on-prem to cloud); client VPNs connect individual devices to a private network. Both rely on IPsec or SSL/TLS.

flashcards.front: Site-to-site VPN vs client VPN — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Site-to-site VPN connects two networks (typical: on-prem data center ↔ cloud VPC) using gateway devices on each side. Client VPN connects an individual user's laptop to a private network for remote access. Site-to-site uses IPsec, client VPN often uses SSL or WireGuard.

flashcards.front: IPsec — IKE phase 1 vs phase 2.
flashcards.back: Phase 1 (IKE) authenticates the two peers (pre-shared key or certificate) and builds a secure management channel. Phase 2 negotiates the actual data tunnel (encryption algorithm, key lifetime). Most exam questions test that phase 1 must succeed before phase 2.

flashcards.front: When do you pick a dedicated link over a VPN?
flashcards.back: VPN over the public internet is cheap but variable — bandwidth and latency depend on internet weather. Dedicated links (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute, Cloud Interconnect) are private fiber with consistent latency and bandwidth — pick them for production traffic that must be predictable, or compliance scenarios that forbid the public internet.

flashcards.front: What's the BGP tunnel option for?
flashcards.back: VPNs can use static routes or BGP. BGP-based VPNs auto-propagate route changes between sides (add a new subnet on-prem → cloud learns it within seconds). Static VPN requires manual route updates every time the topology changes. Always pick BGP for production.

questions.q: An engineer configures a Site-to-Site VPN between AWS and an on-premises router. The VPN tunnel status in the console shows UP but no traffic flows. BGP sessions are ESTABLISHED but no routes are received from AWS. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The Customer Gateway is set with the wrong BGP ASN, which blocks route advertisement to AWS
The IPsec Phase 2 security association is negotiated with mismatched encryption parameters
The security groups on the EC2 instances are dropping the inbound ICMP probes from the on-premises subnet
Route propagation is not enabled on the VPC route table for the Virtual Private Gateway
questions.explanation: When the tunnel is UP and BGP is ESTABLISHED but the VPC route table shows no learned routes, the route table simply isn't accepting them — route propagation from the VGW must be explicitly enabled per route table. A BGP ASN mismatch would prevent the session from reaching ESTABLISHED in the first place. A Phase 2 mismatch would drop the tunnel itself. Security groups affect packet delivery to instances, not what appears in the route table.

questions.q: A company has 2 VPN tunnels to AWS for redundancy but observes asymmetric routing where outbound traffic uses tunnel 1 and return traffic uses tunnel 2, breaking stateful firewalls on-premises. What is the recommended mitigation?
choices: Enable VPN CloudHub on the AWS side so that AWS deterministically forces all return traffic onto the single preferred tunnel
Use AS_PATH prepending or AWS-published BGP communities to set local_preference so both directions prefer the same tunnel
Disable BGP on one of the two tunnels and configure static routing for that path on both ends instead
Enable Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN and turn off ECMP across the two redundant tunnels
questions.explanation: Asymmetric VPN paths are controlled by BGP. On the customer side, AS_PATH prepending makes one tunnel less preferred for inbound traffic; on the AWS side, using AWS-published BGP communities (7224:7100/7200/7300) on the advertised prefixes sets local_preference so AWS prefers the matching tunnel for return traffic. Disabling BGP is a workaround that sacrifices dynamic failover. CloudHub is a separate hub-and-spoke topology. Accelerated VPN improves performance but doesn't fix flow symmetry.

questions.q: A company needs a high-throughput VPN connection (>1.25 Gbps per tunnel, the current S2S VPN limit) to AWS without using Direct Connect. Which solution provides higher throughput VPN to AWS?
choices: Attach multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections to a Transit Gateway and enable ECMP across the tunnels
Use AWS PrivateLink with a VPN overlay built between the producer and the consumer accounts
Use Direct Connect with a hosted VIF that carries the encapsulated VPN payload
Use Client VPN endpoints in a meshed configuration between the router and AWS
questions.explanation: To exceed the per-tunnel ~1.25 Gbps limit without Direct Connect, attach multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections to a Transit Gateway and enable equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) across them — aggregate throughput scales with the number of tunnels. Accelerated VPN improves latency, not per-tunnel bandwidth. PrivateLink isn't a VPN. Client VPN is for remote user access and doesn't form site-to-site mesh.

questions.q: A company configures a Client VPN endpoint with mutual certificate authentication. Users connect successfully, but they cannot reach targets in the associated VPC. Which additional configuration is typically missing?
choices: A wildcard ACM certificate is required on the Client VPN endpoint's server certificate slot before any client can reach the VPC
The client must set its DNS to 8.8.8.8 so that the VPC's internal hostnames resolve
Authorization rules on the Client VPN endpoint that grant access to specific destination CIDRs (plus routes to those CIDRs)
The endpoint must be switched into split-tunnel mode before any VPC traffic can be reached
questions.explanation: AWS Client VPN requires both authorization rules (which users/groups can reach which destination CIDRs) and matching routes on the Client VPN endpoint. A successful connection only proves authentication; without authorization rules, all in-VPC traffic is dropped. DNS server choice doesn't unblock IP reachability. The certificate doesn't need to be a wildcard. Split-tunnel is an optimization (only VPC-destined traffic uses the tunnel), not a prerequisite for reachability.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A company has a Direct Connect connection at 10 Gbps with a private VIF to a single VPC. They now need to connect the same on-premises network to 8 additional VPCs in 3 Regions without provisioning additional DX circuits. What is the most scalable solution?
choices: Create a Direct Connect Gateway, attach a transit VIF, and associate a Transit Gateway in each of the 3 Regions to the DXGW
Provision 8 additional private VIFs on the existing connection, one per VPC, each mapped to that VPC's Virtual Private Gateway
Create a public VIF and run a Site-to-Site VPN over it to each of the additional VPCs, routing through the public AWS service endpoints
Order a hosted VIF for each new VPC and associate every hosted VIF with its own dedicated Virtual Private Gateway
questions.explanation: A Direct Connect Gateway with a transit VIF allows association of Transit Gateways in multiple Regions, reaching all 8 VPCs over the single DX circuit. Per-VPC private VIFs do not scale (each is tied to a single VGW/DXGW) and consume VIF quota. A public VIF over VPN re-introduces internet-style overhead and breaks the DX private path. Hosted VIFs are a billing/ownership model and don't solve the multi-VPC multi-Region requirement.

questions.q: A company needs to connect 5 on-premises data centers to AWS with Direct Connect, and any data center should be able to reach any other data center via AWS as a transit network. Which feature enables this data-center-to-data-center connectivity over AWS?
choices: AWS Cloud WAN with an on-premises Connect attachment configured for each of the five data centers
Direct Connect Gateway with transit VIFs terminating on a central Transit Gateway that relays between the sites
VPN CloudHub with dynamic BGP routing configured between all of the data center sites
AWS Direct Connect SiteLink, which enables any-to-any DX-location connectivity over the AWS global backbone
questions.explanation: AWS Direct Connect SiteLink allows DX connections at any DX location to exchange traffic via the AWS global backbone without needing to traverse a VPC or TGW — it is the purpose-built feature for DC-to-DC transit over AWS. VPN CloudHub works for VPN-only hub-and-spoke and rides the public internet for transport. DXGW + TGW is excellent for VPC connectivity but the path still funnels through a TGW. Cloud WAN focuses on VPC/SD-WAN integration, not pure DX-to-DX transit.

questions.q: A company uses BGP with Direct Connect and wants to influence AWS's outbound routing to prefer one on-premises location over another during normal operations. Which BGP attribute influences AWS route selection from AWS to on-premises?
choices: AWS prefers the route carrying the longest AS_PATH toward the customer specifically in order to avoid hot-potato routing across its own backbone
AWS selects by longest-prefix match first, then local_preference (influenced by communities like 7224:7100/7200/7300), then shortest AS_PATH, then MED
AWS ignores all inbound BGP attributes and always load-balances with ECMP across every available path equally
AWS evaluates only BGP community tags and disregards prefix length entirely when choosing the outbound path
questions.explanation: BGP route selection on the AWS side follows: longest prefix match first, then local_preference (which customers influence via AWS-published BGP communities such as 7224:7100/7200/7300 for low/medium/high preference), then shortest AS_PATH, then MED, then other tiebreakers. The 'longest AS_PATH' option inverts the rule. AWS does honor prefix length, and it doesn't ignore attributes for ECMP unless paths are otherwise equal.

questions.q: A global SaaS provider offers a REST API to customers and needs the lowest possible latency worldwide with anycast static IPs that can be allowlisted in customer firewalls. The backend is an ALB in us-east-1. Which AWS service is most appropriate?
choices: AWS Global Accelerator with the ALB as an endpoint, providing two static anycast IPs routed via the AWS edge network
Amazon CloudFront with the ALB as a custom origin and HTTPS caching behaviors to accelerate the REST API for clients worldwide
Route 53 latency-based routing with health checks that resolve each client to the lowest-latency ALB Region
AWS Direct Connect with a public VIF so customers can reach the ALB over the AWS private backbone
questions.explanation: AWS Global Accelerator provides exactly two static anycast IP addresses that customers can allowlist, then ingests traffic at the nearest AWS edge and rides the AWS backbone to the ALB — minimizing internet hops and latency. CloudFront caches content globally but does not give you static anycast IPs for firewall allowlisting. Route 53 latency-based routing changes DNS responses; the resolved IP varies and isn't a fixed allowlist target. Direct Connect is for private connectivity with specific customers, not a global public-API model.

questions.q: A retail company wants to add automatic failover between two AWS Regions for their application. The application uses Global Accelerator with endpoints in both Regions behind ALBs. Which Global Accelerator feature drives automatic failover?
choices: Global Accelerator requires an operator to manually trigger a CLI failover whenever one of the application Regions becomes unhealthy or unreachable
Global Accelerator uses endpoint group health checks and the traffic dial to shift traffic automatically to healthy endpoint groups
Global Accelerator relies on customer-side BGP advertisements to fail over between the two Regions
Global Accelerator uses Route 53 public hosted zones internally to perform cross-Region failover
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator continuously health-checks endpoints; on failure, traffic is shifted within seconds to healthy endpoint groups based on the traffic dial and weight settings. Because the anycast IPs stay the same, clients don't need DNS re-resolution. It is not a manual failover model, it is not exposed as customer-controlled BGP, and it does not use Route 53 internally for failover.

questions.q: A company is designing a multi-Region active-active architecture with Global Accelerator in front of ALBs in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. They want 70% of traffic to us-east-1 and 30% to eu-west-1. Which Global Accelerator feature controls this split?
choices: Global Accelerator always splits traffic evenly 50/50 across endpoint groups and cannot be tuned
Put Route 53 weighted records in front of the Global Accelerator static IPs to enforce the split
Enable client affinity on the accelerator to pin roughly 70% of clients to the us-east-1 group
Set the endpoint group traffic dial on each Region's endpoint group to achieve the desired 70/30 ratio
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator exposes a 'traffic dial' percentage (0–100) per endpoint group, allowing you to throttle the proportion of traffic that reaches each Region — set the us-east-1 group higher than eu-west-1 to achieve a 70/30 split. Putting Route 53 weighted records in front of Global Accelerator defeats the purpose of static anycast IPs. Client affinity is for session stickiness, not ratio control. The 50/50 claim is simply false.

questions.q: A company runs an HTTPS service behind a Network Load Balancer and wants to preserve the client source IP for logging. The targets are registered by IP (not by instance ID). What must be configured?
choices: Enable Proxy Protocol v2 on the NLB target group so the original client IP is delivered to the targets inside a TLV header
Enable cross-zone load balancing on the NLB so the source IP is preserved as traffic spreads across AZs
Turn on client IP preservation at the listener level and have the application perform its own source NAT
Set the target group attribute 'preserve_client_ip.enabled' to true so the original source IP reaches the targets
questions.explanation: For NLB with IP-type targets, client IP preservation is off by default and is controlled by the target group attribute preserve_client_ip.enabled — set it to true and the original source IP appears at the target. Proxy protocol v2 is an alternative for when you can't or don't want IP preservation (it requires the target application to parse the header). Cross-zone load balancing is about traffic distribution across AZs and has no effect on source IP. There is no listener-level 'preservation' toggle.

questions.q: An application requires UDP-based low-latency real-time gaming traffic. Multiple fleets of EC2 instances act as game servers behind a single load balancer. Which load balancer supports UDP with target groups?
choices: Network Load Balancer with a UDP listener and a matching UDP target group
Classic Load Balancer with the UDP protocol enabled on the front-end listener
Gateway Load Balancer carrying the UDP game traffic over GENEVE to the fleet
Application Load Balancer with a dedicated UDP listener for the gaming fleet
questions.explanation: Network Load Balancer is the only ELB that supports TCP, UDP, and TCP_UDP listeners with corresponding target groups — the standard choice for gaming, DNS, and VoIP. ALB is HTTP/HTTPS-only and has no UDP listener. CLB does not natively support UDP. GWLB transports its own GENEVE-encapsulated traffic on UDP 6081 but is for inline appliances, not as a general-purpose UDP load balancer in front of game servers.
